note: The control arm. Same harness, same five subprocesses per user, same threads and timing calls, with a payload that does no I/O: /usr/bin/true, then node -e 0, then mocactl --version. It touches no cluster. Its purpose is to decide whether local concurrency effects -- process start-up, thread scheduling, the driver host itself -- contaminate the real measurements. Three concurrency levels, 1, 100 and 1000, the last being far above anything a real rung uses (the service caps live sandboxes at 40), so it also locates where the driver host rather than the service becomes the limit.

real_rungs.note: The figure the null arm has to be compared against: the cheapest real CLI row is `ls`, 697 ms at C=1 in the ladder, and the whole six-step lifecycle is 8470 ms at C=1.

predictions.claim: At C=1 the mocactl null tier's per-op p50 is under 300 ms. This is the floor every real CLI row pays before it opens a socket.
At C=1 the mocactl null tier accounts for less than 40% of the cheapest real CLI row (`ls`, 697 ms at C=1), so the majority of even the cheapest real row is not local start-up.
The three tiers are ordered true < node < mocactl at every concurrency level, which is what makes the decomposition meaningful rather than noise.

Local overhead does NOT explain the real ladder's degradation. Going from C=1 to C=100 in the mocactl null tier costs less than 2x on per-op p50 -- and since the real ladder tops out at 40 concurrent users, whatever local growth exists at 100 is an upper bound on what contaminated it.

At C=1000 the mocactl tier degrades sharply -- per-op p50 at least 5x the C=1 value -- because ~1000 concurrent node processes at ~40 MB private each exceed what an 18-core, 64 GB host absorbs. This is a claim about the driver host, not the service, and it is why no real rung is run at that width.
No null operation fails at C=1 or C=100: the host has headroom at the widths the real rungs actually use.
The peak count of genuinely coexisting processes at C=1000 is at least 500, so the level really did test wide concurrency rather than quietly ramping.
